job_heading: The Job: What We Found, What We Did
job_lead: One chimney, start to finish. The detail photos are from the same chimney, taken when the work was done.

found.text: The brick itself was sound. The mortar between the bricks was not: weathered back from the face of the brick, crumbling in places and open to water. That is the usual Toronto story. Freeze-thaw cycles work on the joints first, and once water can get into an open joint, every winter makes it worse.

Left alone, open joints let water into the chimney and, eventually, into the roof structure around it. Bricks start to spall and shift, and a repair becomes a rebuild. Caught at this stage, tuckpointing restores the chimney for a fraction of what a rebuild costs.

steps.title: Inspection and photos
steps.text: The chimney was checked from the roof, joint by joint, and photographed. The homeowner got the photos and the price in writing before anything started.

steps.title: The old mortar cut out
steps.text: Every joint above the roofline was ground back to sound material and the dust blown out, so the new mortar bonds to clean brick rather than to the weathered skin of the old joint.

steps.title: Fresh mortar, packed and tooled
steps.text: The joints were filled in lifts, packed tight, and tooled to a consistent profile. The result in the photo: full, even joints across every face of the chimney.

steps.title: The roofline sealed
steps.text: Where the chimney meets the shingles, the flashing was sealed tight to the brick — the point where most chimney leaks actually start.

steps.title: Clean-up and final photos
steps.text: Roof cleared of debris, and a set of photos of the finished chimney for the homeowner — the one at the top of this page is from that set.

why_lead: When the brick is sound, replacing the mortar is the right repair — and the one that keeps the look of the house.

pillars.title: The original brick stays
pillars.text: Toronto brick from the 1920s to the 1980s is hard to match. Tuckpointing keeps it, so the chimney still looks like it belongs on the house.

pillars.title: Water stops getting in
pillars.text: A closed joint is the whole point. Rain and melting snow run off the chimney instead of into it — and into the attic below.

pillars.title: Done once, done early
pillars.text: Mortar is the part of a chimney designed to wear first. Replacing it on time is routine work; waiting turns it into brick replacement or a rebuild.

faq.a: Tuckpointing (also called repointing) is cutting the old, weathered mortar out of the joints between the bricks and filling them with fresh mortar. The brick stays. It is the standard repair for a chimney whose mortar has worn before the brick has.

faq.q: How do I know if my chimney needs tuckpointing?
faq.a: Look at the joints from the ground with a zoom lens or binoculars: mortar that has receded behind the face of the brick, gaps, or sandy mortar you can scrape out with a key are the signs. White staining on the brick and water marks near the fireplace are signs water is already getting in. Our free inspection checks every joint from the roof and photographs them for you.

faq.q: Do you match the colour of the mortar?
faq.a: As closely as the original allows. Mortar colour depends on the sand and the mix; we match the mix to the age and style of the house so the new joints blend in once they have cured. Fresh mortar always looks lighter for the first few weeks.

faq.q: Can tuckpointing be done in winter?
faq.a: Mortar needs to cure above freezing, so the work is done in the warmer months. If you notice open joints in winter, book the inspection now — we photograph and price the work, and schedule it for the first suitable weather.

faq.q: What does tuckpointing cost in Toronto?
faq.a: It depends on the size of the chimney and how much of it needs repointing — which is exactly what the free inspection establishes. You get the price in writing before any work starts. See how we price the work.
